Since 2014, the [government of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Government of the People's Republic of China") has committed a series of ongoing [human rights abuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights#Violations "Human rights") against [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") and other [Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_peoples "Turkic peoples") Muslim minorities in [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") which has often been characterized as [persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution "Persecution") or as [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide"). There have been reports of mass [arbitrary arrests and detention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary_arrest_and_detention "Arbitrary arrest and detention"), [torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture"), [mass surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance "Mass surveillance"), cultural and religious persecution, [family separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_separation "Family separation"), [forced labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor"), [sexual violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_violence "Sexual violence"), and violations of [reproductive rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproductive_rights "Reproductive rights").

In 2014, the [administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping_Administration "Xi Jinping Administration") of [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) [general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") launched the [Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Hard_Campaign_Against_Violent_Terrorism "Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism"), which involved surveillance and restrictions in Xinjiang. Beginning in 2017, under [Xinjiang Party secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_Secretary_of_Xinjiang "Party Secretary of Xinjiang") [Chen Quanguo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Quanguo "Chen Quanguo"),[[2]](#cite_note-Khatchadourian-5-4-2021-2) the government incarcerated over an estimated one million Uyghurs without [legal process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_process "Legal process") in [internment camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps "Xinjiang internment camps") officially described as "vocational education and training centers", in the largest mass internment of an ethnic-religious minority group since [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[3]](#cite_note-Finley-2020-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) China began to wind down the camps in 2019, and some detainees were transferred to the [penal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_system_in_China "Penal system in China"), while others were transferred to [forced labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor") and factory work programs.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In addition to mass detention, government policies have included suppression of Uyghur [religious practices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_China "Islam in China"),[[7]](#cite_note-7) political [indoctrination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indoctrination "Indoctrination"),[[8]](#cite_note-reut_Musl-8) [forced sterilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_sterilization "Forced sterilization"),[[9]](#cite_note-apne_Chin-9) forced [contraception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraception "Contraception"),[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-genocide_against_the_Uyghurs-11) and [forced abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_abortion "Forced abortion").[[12]](#cite_note-urlwww.dw.com-12)[[13]](#cite_note-bbc-13) An estimated 16,000 [mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") have been razed or damaged,[[2]](#cite_note-Khatchadourian-5-4-2021-2) and hundreds of thousands of children have been forcibly separated from their parents and sent to [boarding schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_schools_in_China "Boarding schools in China").[[14]](#cite_note-2018FTFamily-14)[[15]](#cite_note-:1-15) Since 2017, preferential [family planning exemptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_planning_policies_of_China#Ethnic_minority_policies "Family planning policies of China") previously available to Uyghurs have reportedly been reduced or removed.[[16]](#cite_note-:11-16)[[17]](#cite_note-:10-17) Chinese government statistics reported that from 2015 to 2018, [birth rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_rate "Birth rate") in the mostly Uyghur regions of [Hotan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotan "Hotan") and [Kashgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashgar "Kashgar") fell by more than 60%.[[9]](#cite_note-apne_Chin-9) In the same period, the national birth rate decreased by 9.7%.[[18]](#cite_note-data_Birt-18) According to *CNN*, Chinese authorities acknowledged that birth rates dropped by almost a third in 2018 in Xinjiang, but denied reports of forced sterilization.[[19]](#cite_note-cnn-fax-19) Birth rates in Xinjiang fell a further 24% in 2019, compared to a nationwide decrease of 4.2%.[[9]](#cite_note-apne_Chin-9)

The Chinese government denies having committed human rights abuses in Xinjiang.[[3]](#cite_note-Finley-2020-3)[[20]](#cite_note-20) International reactions have varied, with its actions being described as the [forced assimilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_assimilation "Forced assimilation") of Xinjiang, as [ethnocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnocide "Ethnocide") or [cultural genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_genocide "Cultural genocide"),[[21]](#cite_note-indy-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22) or as genocide. Those accusing China of genocide point to intentional acts they say violate [Article II of the Genocide Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_Convention#Definition_of_genocide "Genocide Convention"),[[23]](#cite_note-BBC_News-2021-23)[[24]](#cite_note-icij_Brit-24)[[25]](#cite_note-Piotrowicz-25) which prohibits "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part", a "racial or religious group" including "causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group" and "measures intended to prevent births within the group".[[26]](#cite_note-Convention-text-26)

At the United Nations, several countries, predominantly in North America and Europe, signed letters condemning China's policies. On the other hand, several countries, predominantly in Asia and Africa, signed letters supporting the policies as an effort to combat terrorism in the region.[[27]](#cite_note-:53-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29) In 2020, a case brought to the [International Criminal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Court "International Criminal Court") was dismissed because China is not a party to the [Rome Statute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome_Statute "Rome Statute"), meaning the ICC could not investigate them.[[30]](#cite_note-:0-30) I

The **Hong Kong 47** is a group of 47 [pro-democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-democracy_camp_(Hong_Kong) "Pro-democracy camp (Hong Kong)") advocates in [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") charged with conspiracy to commit [subversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subversion "Subversion") under the [Hong Kong national security law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Hong_Kong_national_security_law "2020 Hong Kong national security law").[[1]](#cite_note-ft_20220623-1)

On 6 January 2021, 53 activists, former legislators, social workers and academics were arrested by the [National Security Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Department "National Security Department") of the [Hong Kong Police Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Police_Force "Hong Kong Police Force") under the national security law over their organisation and participation in the [primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Hong_Kong_pro-democracy_primaries "2020 Hong Kong pro-democracy primaries") for the [subsequently postponed Legislative Council election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postponement_of_the_2020_Hong_Kong_legislative_election "Postponement of the 2020 Hong Kong legislative election"), including six organisers and 48 participants, of which two were arrested in jail, making it the largest crackdown under the national security law since its passage on 30 June 2020. Authorities also raided 72 sites including the home of jailed activist [Joshua Wong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Wong "Joshua Wong"), the offices of news outlets *[Apple Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Daily "Apple Daily")*, *[Stand News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand_News "Stand News")* and [Hong Kong Inmedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Inmedia "Hong Kong Inmedia"); and polling institute [Hong Kong Public Opinion Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Public_Opinion_Research_Institute "Hong Kong Public Opinion Research Institute") (PORI), and froze more than $200,000 in funds related to the primaries.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The arrests reduced the pro-democracy camp, including its moderate wing, considerably, and targeted several prominent figures.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

On 28 February 2021, 47 opposition figures among those arrested in January were officially charged with conspiracy to commit subversion under the national security law. Their appearance in court on 1 March saw hundreds of protesters assembling outside the building.[[4]](#cite_note-nytimes_20210301-4)

Several defence lawyers expressed their objections in court to the slow prosecutions, which contrasted with speedily pressed charges.[[4]](#cite_note-nytimes_20210301-4) Analysts considered the slow trial, which extended to other national security cases, to be a deliberate strategy designed to stoke fear.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The case was adjourned several times; at the adjournment on 4 March 2022, the next hearing date was set as 28 April, due to the COVID-19 pandemic,[[6]](#cite_note-hkfp_20220304-6) at which date the defendants were told to appear again on 1 to 2 June; a higher court judge had called on the handling lower court a few days earlier to deliver a speedy trial.[[7]](#cite_note-hkfp_20220429-7) The defendants were subjected at times to solitary confinement.[[1]](#cite_note-ft_20220623-1)

The trial lasted from 6 February to 4 December 2023.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-hkfp_20231204-9) Two were acquitted by the panel of judges in May 2024, while the remaining 14 were found guilty. Along with 31 defendants who had entered a plea deal, the sentences of the 45 ranged from 4 years and 2 months to 10 years in prison. [Benny Tai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Tai "Benny Tai"), whom the court described as the "mastermind" for initiating the plan, was handed the longest jail term. As of 1 February 2026, 18 of the sentenced have been released.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/DSCF8440_%2850104989307%29.jpg/250px-DSCF8440_%2850104989307%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DSCF8440_(50104989307).jpg)

Long queue outside polling station at [Tai Po Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tai_Po_Plaza "Tai Po Plaza") on 12 July 2020

On 11 and 12 July 2020, the pro-democracy camp, organised by legal scholar and activist [Benny Tai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Tai "Benny Tai"), held a primary to select numbers of candidates for the [September Legislative Council election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Hong_Kong_legislative_election "2020 Hong Kong legislative election") to maximise the chance for the pro-democrats to achieve the "35+" majority in the [Legislative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Council_of_Hong_Kong "Legislative Council of Hong Kong") to block the government's bills and pressured the government to implement the [five key demands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%932020_Hong_Kong_protests#Objectives "2019–2020 Hong Kong protests") of the [ongoing protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%932020_Hong_Kong_protests "2019–2020 Hong Kong protests").[[11]](#cite_note-11) Tai envisaged that the democrats would veto all bills in the legislature to paralyse the government, and would force the [Chief Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Executive_of_Hong_Kong "Chief Executive of Hong Kong") to dissolve the Legislative Council after the government budget was vetoed, as on the fourth and fifth stages of the "ten-step [lam chau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lam_chau_(doctrine) "Lam chau (doctrine)")" timeline.[[12]](#cite_note-12) The resignation of the Chief Executive would be forced by Article 52 of the Basic Law if the Legislative Council resulting from a by-election still did not approve the budget.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

# Lens 2B.5 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler restrain security forces, militias, allies, proxies, clients, and arms recipients from atrocities or destabilization, and accept responsibility for foreseeable proxy conduct?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative**. Xi did not restrain Chinese security forces in Xinjiang (mass internment / forced-labor apparatus continued under his August 2023 "success" declaration), Hong Kong (NSL trial of 47 pro-democracy politicians in 2023; Jimmy Lai's trial scheduled), Tibet, or against human-rights lawyers and journalists; did not restrain allies on WMD proliferation (Russia nuclear coercion un-restrained; DPRK sanctions un-enforced; Iran JCPOA revival declined; Pakistan nuclear continued; Syria CW compliance declined); did not restrain client regimes on atrocities (Syria's Assad received 22 September 2023 partnership without CW conditionality); and did not accept responsibility for any foreseeable proxy conduct — the 2023 public record shows no Chinese accountability for, or public distancing from, ally or proxy conduct that amounted to atrocities or destabilization.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — Chinese security forces unrestrained in 2023

### 1. Xinjiang mass-internment / forced-labor apparatus continued under Xi's "success" declaration

- **Claim A1.** In August 2023, Xi visited Xinjiang and publicly declared his policies there a "success." The mass-internment / forced-labor apparatus (up to 1.8 million Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims detained in internment camps, with continued forcible labor, family separation, and cultural-religious repression; the OHCHR report of August 2022 found that "acts indicating that crimes against humanity may have been committed" by China) continued. The 2023 internment-camp and forced-labor framework was not moderated, was not opened to independent inspection, and was publicly celebrated by Xi. This is a failure to restrain one's own security forces.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In August, President Xi visited Xinjiang ahead of the first anniversary of a damning United Nations report that detailed widespread abuses across Xinjiang—including targeting of cultural and religious practices, family separation, arbitrary arrests and detention, rapes, torture, and enforced disappearances—and concluded that Beijing's policies in the region 'may constitute crimes against humanity.' Xi pronounced that his policies in Xinjiang were a 'success' … In September, a court sentenced prominent Uyghur anthropologist Dr. Rahile Dawut to life imprisonment").
  - **Source:** "Xinjiang internment camps" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps ("mass internments peaked in 2018 and have abated somewhat since then, with officials shifting focus towards forced labor programs … the internment of Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims in the camps constituted the largest-scale arbitrary detention of an ethnic and religious minorities since World War II").
  - **Source:** "Uyghur genocide" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghur_genocide (records 2014–present atrocities, the Xi-administration origin, and the OHCHR determination that crimes against humanity may have been committed).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.5 (strongly negative — own security forces unrestrained), 2B.4, 8D.5.

### 2. Hong Kong NSL prosecutions continued throughout 2023

- **Claim A2.** In 2023, the Hong Kong 47 national-security trial proceeded (trial lasted from 6 February to 4 December 2023). Jimmy Lai's national-security trial was scheduled for 18 December 2023. In October 2023, four former university student leaders were sentenced to two years in prison. In July 2023, Hong Kong police issued baseless arrest warrants and bounties on eight exiled activists abroad. The NSL prosecution rate was ~100%. This is a failure to restrain Hong Kong security apparatus in 2023.
  - **Source:** "Hong Kong 47" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_47 ("The trial lasted from 6 February to 4 December 2023 … 45 jailed (31 pleaded guilty, 14 found guilty) … Imprisonment of 4 years 2 months to 10 years").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In July, the high-profile national security trial of 47 pro-democracy politicians began. Another national security trial, of 75-year-old media tycoon Jimmy Lai, was slated to begin on December 18. In October, four former university student leaders were sentenced to two years in prison for 'incitement to wound with intent.' … In July, police issued baseless arrest warrants and bounties on eight exiled politicians and activists who reside abroad for offenses under the National Security Law. Police froze their bank accounts, interrogated their Hong Kong-based family members, and raided the homes of activists associated with them").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.5 (negative — Hong Kong security unrestrained), 2B.4, 8D.6.

### 3. Human-rights lawyers and journalists prosecuted throughout 2023

- **Claim A3.** Throughout 2023, Chinese authorities continued to prosecute human-rights lawyers and journalists at scale: Xu Zhiyong (14 years), Ding Jiaxi (12 years), Guo Feixiong (8 years), Qin Yongpei (5 years), Yang Shaozheng (4.5 years), Yu Wensheng and his wife Xu Yan (arrested in April 2023 en route to a meeting with the EU ambassador), Wang Quanzhang / Wang Yu / Bao Longjun (house arrest), journalist Yang Zewei (disappeared from Laos in May 2023, reappeared in Hunan detention), and human-rights lawyer Lu Siwei (deported from Laos to China in September 2023). The pattern shows a security apparatus unrestrained by the central political authority.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.5 (negative — own security forces unrestrained), 2B.4, 8D.7.

### 4. Tibetan and minority-religious repression continued

- **Claim A4.** Throughout 2023, Tibetan religious and political repression continued. A revered Tibetan monk (Geshe Phende Gyaltsen, arrested 2022) died in police custody in January 2023. In June 2023, UN special rapporteurs requested information about six Tibetans detained for possession of photos of the Dalai Lama. The Religious Activity Venues Measures (September 2023) imposed CCP indoctrination on religious groups and Sinicized Islam (closure / demolition of mosques in Ningxia, Yunnan). This is a failure to restrain religious-repression forces.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.5 (negative — own security forces unrestrained), 8D.4, 8D.5.

### 5. Counterespionage Law (effective July 2023) — state authority over civilians expanded

- **Claim A5.** The revised Counterespionage Law (effective July 2023) expanded state authority to inspect electronic equipment and data, restricted information transmission about national security, and was followed by a Ministry of State Security call to citizens to engage in counterespionage activity. This is a structural expansion of state authority that empowers security forces against civilians, not a restraint.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.5 (negative — security forces empowered), 2B.4, 1B.9.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — proxy / ally / client restraint declined in 2023

### 6. Russia nuclear-coercion rhetoric unrestrained by Xi

- **Claim A6.** Throughout 2023, Russia suspended New START (21 February), withdrew CTBT ratification (November), stationed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus, and made repeated nuclear-coercion threats against NATO. Xi did **not** publicly distance himself from Russia's nuclear-coercion rhetoric or use Chinese leverage to restrain it. On 17 October 2023, Xi hosted Putin at the 3rd Belt and Road Forum and provided a high-profile platform for Putin's first meeting with an EU leader (Hungarian PM Orbán) since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. This is a failure to restrain an ally on atrocities-equivalent nuclear coercion.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("17 October – Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold talks at the Belt and Road Initiative forum in Beijing. It is the first meeting between Putin and an EU leader since Russia's invasion of Ukraine").
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START ("On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START").
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty ("In 2023, in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian war, Russia withdrew its ratification of the CTBT").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.5 (strongly negative — ally unrestrained), 1B.4, 1B.6, 8G.7.

### 7. DPRK nuclear advancement unrestrained by Chinese sanctions enforcement

- **Claim A7.** Throughout 2023, China — as a permanent UNSC member and key DPRK trade partner — continued limited enforcement of UN Security Council sanctions on the DPRK. The DPRK continued its nuclear-program advancement and ballistic-missile testing (Hwasong-18 solid-fuel ICBM in April 2023, additional tests). Xi did **not** push for new UNSC sanctions or visibly tighten bilateral enforcement. This is a failure to restrain a nuclear-proliferating ally.

## D. Net reading for lens 2B.5

The 2023 evidence is **strongly negative** on the question of restraint and acceptance of responsibility:

- **Own security forces unrestrained:** Xinjiang mass internment, Hong Kong NSL trials, human-rights lawyer and journalist prosecutions, Tibetan / Hui / religious-minority repression, Counterespionage Law expansion — all continued or intensified in 2023 under Xi's direct authority.
- **Allies unrestrained:** Russia nuclear-coercion rhetoric; DPRK nuclear advancement via Chinese sanctions non-enforcement; Iran nuclear non-restraint; Pakistan nuclear and missile expansion; Syria CW use with no conditionality.
- **Client regimes unrestrained:** Syria's Assad received Belt and Road partnership in September 2023 without CW compliance; surveillance-tech export to authoritarian regimes continued.
- **No acceptance of responsibility:** no public Xi statement in 2023 accepting Chinese responsibility for any proxy or ally conduct.
- **Partial positives:** no new kinetic war; India LAC architecture held; mil-to-mil reset; Iran–Saudi rapprochement.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have (a) opened Xinjiang to independent inspection, (b) accepted international NSL-procedural critique in Hong Kong, (c) conditioned Russia partnership on nuclear-coercion restraint, (d) tightened DPRK sanctions, (e) conditioned Iran on JCPOA revival, (f) conditioned Syria on CW compliance, (g) joined the April 2023 multilateral surveillance-tech export-control framework, and (h) accepted some Chinese responsibility for foreseeable ally or proxy conduct. Xi did the opposite on each.

**Net judgment: 2B.5 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi did not restrain his own security forces, did not restrain allies on atrocities or destabilization, did not restrain client regimes, and did not accept responsibility for foreseeable proxy conduct. The partial positives (Iran–Saudi, mil-to-mil) are outweighed by the multi-theater restraint failures.**
